projects.name: Cloud-Backed Portfolio
projects.summary: A React and TypeScript portfolio on GitHub Pages backed by Python 3.11 Azure Functions for health, visitor counting, and a provider-neutral AI assistant.
projects.purpose: A small, cost-conscious portfolio platform that also demonstrates cloud and DevOps engineering through serverless APIs, Infrastructure as Code, automated delivery, observability, and deployment verification.
projects.status_detail: Live system and source-controlled project. The frontend is published at https://jeysibn.github.io/.
projects.experience_boundary: Personal portfolio project; it demonstrates production-oriented engineering practices but is not professional employment experience.

architecture.frontend: React and TypeScript single-page application built with Vite. The generated artifact is published to the Jeysibn/jeysibn.github.io repository and served by GitHub Pages.
architecture.backend: Python 3.11 Azure Functions using the Python v2 programming model.
architecture.state: Azure Cosmos DB NoSQL API with PortfolioDB, Counter, and VisitorIPs containers. Visitor and rate-limit identifiers are HMAC-derived before persistence; VisitorIPs has a 24-hour TTL.
architecture.infrastructure: Terraform with AzureRM in Azure Korea Central; remote Terraform state is stored in Azure Blob Storage.
architecture.delivery: GitHub Actions validates changes, uses GitHub OIDC federation with Microsoft Entra ID for Azure, publishes the frontend to the Pages repository, and runs backend smoke checks after deployment.
architecture.observability: Workspace-based Application Insights and Log Analytics capture request, latency, failure, exception, and structured operational telemetry.
architecture.assistant: The portfolio-specific assistant uses an OpenAI-compatible provider behind the backend; provider secrets remain server-side and the frontend uses neutral branding.

security_decisions: GitHub Actions uses short-lived OIDC tokens for Azure instead of a reusable Azure service-principal secret.
Visitor IPs are never persisted in plaintext; HMAC-derived identifiers support counting and rate limiting.
Request validation, bounded history, backend-authoritative hourly quota, and response sanitization protect the public assistant endpoint.
Secrets and Terraform state are kept outside the frontend bundle and public knowledge content.
projects.ci_cd: Development validation covers frontend typecheck/build, backend Ruff/pytest, and Terraform validation. Main merges use path-specific frontend, backend, and infrastructure deployment workflows with post-deployment verification.
projects.infrastructure: GitHub Pages, Azure Functions on the Consumption plan, Azure Cosmos DB, Application Insights, Log Analytics, Azure Blob Storage for Terraform state, and Azure Korea Central resources managed by Terraform.
projects.observability: Application Insights and Log Analytics receive Azure Function telemetry and privacy-conscious structured assistant events; deployment workflows also verify the health and visitor-counter endpoints.
projects.data_storage: Cosmos DB stores the visitor counter and per-visitor rate-limit records. The frontend stores only the browser chat history and an opaque session routing identifier in sessionStorage.
engineering_decisions: Serverless consumption hosting avoids an always-on application server for a low-traffic portfolio.
Behavior instructions stay separate from approved factual content so prompt changes and portfolio facts can be reviewed independently.
Runtime readiness is checked after deployment rather than inferred from package upload success.
operational_lessons: Optional provider configuration must initialize lazily so unrelated Function routes remain indexable.
Operational telemetry should contain metadata rather than secrets or full visitor conversations.
Deployment success and dependency-backed runtime health are separate signals.
limitations: The assistant depends on an external OpenAI-compatible provider and can be temporarily unavailable.
The AI question quota is per HMAC-derived visitor identity and hour, not a strict browser-session quota.
The portfolio corpus is small and currently uses deterministic retrieval; vector search is intentionally deferred.
claims_not_to_make: Do not describe this as a high-scale or revenue-producing production platform.
Do not claim the assistant has live repository retrieval or a vector database.
Do not expose API keys, visitor IPs, Terraform state, or internal provider configuration.

projects.name: Homelab GitOps Environment
projects.summary: A single-node k3s environment on a Terraform-provisioned Proxmox VM, with Calico bootstrap, Argo CD convergence, LAN ingress, storage, DNS, and observability.
projects.purpose: A personal home-lab environment for applying declarative infrastructure, Kubernetes, GitOps delivery, continuous validation, and operational visibility.
projects.status_detail: Active personal engineering project with a current single-node K3s topology.
projects.experience_boundary: Personal home-lab project, not professional production Kubernetes employment experience.

architecture.virtualization: Terraform provisions an Ubuntu virtual machine on a refurbished/repurposed Proxmox host.
architecture.cluster: K3s currently runs as a single-node Kubernetes server. Calico provides pod networking; overlay encapsulation is disabled for this topology.
architecture.gitops: Argo CD uses an App-of-Apps structure and sync waves to reconcile workloads from the main branch.
architecture.networking: MetalLB provides LoadBalancer IP management, Traefik provides ingress, and Cert-Manager handles TLS. Pi-hole, Unbound, and ExternalDNS provide DNS-related services.
architecture.storage: Longhorn provides CSI-backed persistent volumes, but high availability claims must be qualified because the cluster is single-node.
architecture.observability: Prometheus, Loki, Alloy, and Grafana provide metrics, logs, collection, and visualization.
architecture.remote_access: A Raspberry Pi 4B provides remote access through Tailscale and is not currently a Kubernetes node.

projects.ci_cd: GitHub Actions validates shell scripts, YAML, rendered Helm applications, Kubernetes schemas, and Terraform. After merge, Argo CD detects drift and reconciles the cluster from main.
projects.infrastructure: Proxmox, Terraform, Ubuntu, K3s, Calico, Argo CD, Helm, MetalLB, Traefik, Cert-Manager, Longhorn, Pi-hole, Unbound, Prometheus, Loki, Alloy, and Grafana.
projects.observability: Prometheus collects metrics, Loki stores logs, Alloy routes telemetry, and Grafana provides operational dashboards for the homelab platform.
projects.data_storage: Longhorn-backed Kubernetes persistent volumes are used by stateful workloads; repository documentation also describes the service and storage topology.
security_decisions: Bootstrap owns K3s and Calico because Argo CD requires a working network and DNS before it can reconcile.
The repository separates bootstrap infrastructure from Argo-managed platform/application services.
Some application credentials remain placeholders; future secret management is documented as work for SOPS, Sealed Secrets, or External Secrets.
engineering_decisions: Network acceptance checks run before Argo CD installation.
The current single-node topology avoids Calico overlay encapsulation after a documented UDP Service/NAT incident.
The App-of-Apps registry keeps chart versions, values, namespaces, and sync waves reviewable in Git.
operational_lessons: A blanket Calico UDP NOTRACK rule broke UDP Service NAT even while pod routing and TCP Service traffic worked.
Mixed CPU architectures in an earlier laptop/Raspberry Pi experiment exposed compatibility concerns.
The repository documents an intended under-15-minute rebuild path, but that duration is not a measured personal benchmark.
A single-node cluster is useful for learning and repeatability but is not equivalent to a highly available production cluster.
limitations: Current Kubernetes topology is one node, so it has no node-level high availability.
Some credentials and deployment-owner work remain placeholders or documented gaps.
The under-15-minute recovery target is documented intent, not a verified measured result.
claims_not_to_make: Do not describe it as Jerome professionally operating enterprise Kubernetes.
Do not call the single-node cluster highly available.
Do not call the Raspberry Pi a current K3s node.
Do not state that the rebuild time has been personally benchmarked.

projects.name: MoniKey
projects.summary: A self-hosted personal finance application with a React frontend, Fastify API, PostgreSQL ledger, and a separate worker for durable background work.
projects.purpose: A privacy-first, self-hosted personal finance application where exact ledger values, explicit review, local-first boundaries, and operational recovery matter.
projects.status_detail: Active engineering project; deployment documentation records remaining gaps and it should not be presented as a production service.

architecture.frontend: React 19 and Vite served by nginx.
architecture.storage: PostgreSQL 18 is authoritative for finance state and durable worker state. Ledger money remains PostgreSQL BIGINT and crosses the JSON boundary as decimal minor-unit strings.
architecture.worker: A separate worker uses PostgreSQL-backed durable jobs, shares the backend codebase and database, claims due rows from worker_jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, retries failed work, recovers stale locks, and records terminal dead states.
architecture.local_first: IndexedDB-backed cached snapshots, receipt blobs, pending create intentions, and explicit replay/discard choices are bounded local-first features. Browser Tesseract OCR returns suggestions and does not post transactions.
architecture.adapters: Provider-neutral seams cover FX, crypto quotes, OCR, AI insights, object storage, email, and bank imports; optional adapters still require configuration and user review.

projects.ci_cd: The repository uses GitHub Actions for Node 24/PostgreSQL 18 validation, migrations, tests, integration checks, security scanning, and publication of application and migration images. The external homelab GitOps repository owns deployment manifests and rollout configuration.
projects.infrastructure: Docker/Compose, nginx, PostgreSQL 18, a Fastify API, a separate worker, and external GitOps deployment configuration.
security_decisions: Argon2id password hashing, hashed random session tokens, HttpOnly/SameSite cookies, Secure production cookies, origin enforcement, rate limiting, request IDs, and redacted logs are implemented.
Plaid is sandbox-only in the documented adapter boundary.
Secrets and provider credentials remain deployment configuration rather than repository content.
projects.observability: The repository includes request IDs, redacted logging, health/metrics modules, worker lifecycle handling, and operational documentation.
projects.data_storage: PostgreSQL stores authoritative users, accounts, transactions, budgets, goals, recurring items, imports, reconciliation, investment/crypto data, notification outbox rows, and worker jobs. Receipt files use a separate storage path and need separate backup handling.
engineering_decisions: PostgreSQL-backed durable scheduling avoids adding a message broker for the worker use case.
BIGINT minor units and decimal strings avoid floating-point arithmetic at the money boundary.
Adapters keep external integrations replaceable and make stubs usable in CI.
operational_lessons: Durable job state, stale-lock recovery, retries, and a terminal dead state make background work diagnosable.
The repository documents that PostgreSQL and receipt files require separate backups.
Current deployment notes still identify mutable image references, HTTP/development configuration, and missing backup wiring as gaps.
limitations: The project is active development rather than a claim of production operation.
Some UI workflows and external adapters remain disabled, optional, sandboxed, or require provider configuration and user review.
Deployment digest, secure transport, and backup wiring gaps remain documented work.
claims_not_to_make: Do not claim MoniKey uses RabbitMQ for its worker scheduler; it uses PostgreSQL durable jobs and SKIP LOCKED.
Do not claim every optional adapter or free-form AI question workflow is enabled.
Do not present the application as handling real production financial data.

projects.name: NOC Report Builder
projects.summary: An evolving NOC report builder that turns shift-scoped incidents and frozen evidence into validated analysis and deterministic web/DOCX reports.
projects.purpose: An evolving NOC report builder that keeps operational evidence traceable while bounding AI to supported narrative reasoning.
projects.status_detail: Active development project; repository maturity and current limitations should be stated rather than implying production deployment.

architecture.frontend: React and TypeScript with Vite, Vitest, and Tailwind.
architecture.api: FastAPI routes cover authentication/RBAC, shifts, incidents, evidence, OCR, jobs, analysis, reports, search, analytics, and administration.
architecture.persistence: PostgreSQL stores domain state, provenance, jobs, snapshots, and report metadata; MinIO stores immutable evidence and generated artifacts.
architecture.queue: Transactional outbox rows are committed with jobs before RabbitMQ dispatch. RabbitMQ carries references rather than evidence bytes.
architecture.ai_execution: A host-side Claude Code Bridge resolves the exact SkillSnapshot and executes skills inside a Docker sandbox with validation and bounded usage.
architecture.composition: Report Composition owns mandatory coverage, ordering, provenance, and evidence. Claude produces a narrative-only ReportPlan, and a renderer-neutral ReportDocument feeds web preview and DOCX output.

projects.ci_cd: The repository includes automated validation, unit/integration coverage, sandbox/bridge checks, and gated live benchmarks; the project remains under active development.
projects.infrastructure: React/Vite, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, MinIO, RabbitMQ, a Claude Code Bridge, and Docker sandbox execution.
security_decisions: SkillSnapshot hashes and schema validation preserve execution identity.
Object-reference allow-lists prevent generated results from inventing evidence references.
Job leases, retry/dead-letter controls, bounded AI use, RBAC, and provenance tracking constrain operational automation.
projects.observability: Jobs, analysis runs, report metadata, evidence provenance, request IDs, and execution snapshots provide traceability across the workflow.
projects.data_storage: PostgreSQL is the domain/provenance store; MinIO stores evidence and report/job artifacts; RabbitMQ carries durable job messages and references.
engineering_decisions: The application, not Claude, derives mandatory report facts from the frozen ReportSnapshot.
A renderer-neutral semantic document keeps web and DOCX output consistent.
The job/outbox transaction prevents dispatching work that was not durably recorded.
operational_lessons: AI is most trustworthy when evidence, coverage, and composition remain application-owned.
Reference allow-lists and snapshot hashes make generated analysis explainable and reproducible.
A queue message should identify frozen evidence rather than copying the evidence payload.
limitations: The repository is active development and does not establish a production NOC deployment claim.
Claude owns supported narrative reasoning only; it does not determine mandatory report facts or evidence coverage.
Some benchmark and execution paths are deliberately gated because they consume external model usage.
claims_not_to_make: Do not say Claude determines mandatory report facts; deterministic Report Composition does.
Do not confuse this project's RabbitMQ queue with MoniKey's PostgreSQL worker scheduler.
Do not claim a production NOC service or measured operational outcome without repository evidence.
